specPoints.text: understand how abiotic and biotic factors affect the population size and distribution of organisms

primer.text: Every environmental pressure is either living or non-living. This note sorts the two families, then shows how abiotic factors like light, temperature, water, soil and oxygen, and biotic factors like food, predators, pathogens and competition, decide where organisms survive and how many persist.

lessons.title: Sorting the Factors
lessons.opening: Ecologists split every environmental pressure into two families: abiotic factors are the non-living conditions such as temperature, light intensity and wind speed, while biotic factors are the living pressures such as competition, predation and disease.
keyPoints: An abiotic factor is a non-living part of the environment.
Examples of abiotic factors include temperature, light intensity and wind speed.
A biotic factor is a living pressure within the environment.
Examples of biotic factors include competition, predation and disease.

low.restatement: If it is alive or came from something alive, it is biotic; everything else is abiotic.
low.analogy: A school photo: the weather and the building set the scene, the other pupils set the pressure.
low.examPointer: Learn three examples of each — temperature, light, wind for abiotic; competition, predation, disease for biotic.

medium.restatement: The split is about origin: abiotic factors are physical and chemical conditions, while biotic factors arise from other organisms, whether they are competing with you, eating you or infecting you; both families shape population size and distribution together.
medium.analogy: A football match: the pitch and weather are abiotic, the opposing team is biotic.
medium.examPointer: In classification questions, justify with the word living or non-living, not with vague size or importance.

check.stem: Which list contains only abiotic factors?

options.text: Temperature, light intensity and wind speed
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

options.text: Predation, competition and disease
options.explanation: All three are living pressures, so biotic.

options.text: Food supply and pathogens
options.explanation: Food and pathogens involve living organisms.

options.text: Grazing and pollination
options.explanation: Grazing and pollination are biotic interactions.

check.stem: What defines a biotic factor?

options.text: It is a living pressure in the environment
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: It is any chemical in the soil
options.explanation: Chemicals alone are abiotic; life defines biotic.

options.text: It is weather measured daily
options.explanation: Weather is non-living, so abiotic.

options.text: It is any factor humans measure
options.explanation: Measurement has nothing to do with the split.

check.stem: Wind speed over a sand dune is which kind of factor?

options.text: Abiotic, because wind is non-living
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: Biotic, because it moves living sand grains
options.explanation: Sand is not alive; wind stays abiotic.

options.text: Biotic, because plants respond to it
options.explanation: Responses do not make the factor living.

options.text: Neither category applies
options.explanation: Wind speed is a textbook abiotic factor.

check.stem: Ash dieback disease sweeping through a woodland is which factor?

options.text: Biotic, because a living pathogen drives it
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

options.text: Abiotic, because spores are tiny
options.explanation: Size does not decide; the fungus is living.

options.text: Abiotic, because weather spreads spores
options.explanation: Weather only carries the living cause.

options.text: Neither, disease is human-made
options.explanation: Natural disease is a classic biotic factor.

check.stem: Why do ecologists separate the two factor families?

options.text: Because living and non-living pressures shape populations through different mechanisms
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: Because one family matters more always
options.explanation: Both matter; the split is about mechanism.

options.text: Because exams demand two lists
options.explanation: The split reflects real ecological causation.

options.text: Because factors never interact
options.explanation: They interact constantly; classification aids analysis.

check.stem: State the meaning of the term abiotic factor.
check.modelAnswer: An abiotic factor is a non-living part of the environment, such as temperature or light intensity.

check.stem: State the meaning of the term biotic factor.
check.modelAnswer: A biotic factor is a living pressure within the environment, such as competition, predation or disease.

check.stem: Explain why light intensity is classed as abiotic while food supply is biotic.
check.modelAnswer: Light intensity is abiotic because light is non-living, while food supply is biotic because the food is made of living or once-living organisms.

check.stem: A drought dries a pond while herons arrive to fish. Classify both pressures.
check.modelAnswer: The drought is abiotic, being a non-living water shortage, while the herons are biotic, being living predators on the pond organisms.

lessons.title: Non-Living Limits
sourceHeadings: How abiotic factors affect population size and distribution
lessons.opening: Non-living conditions decide where organisms can live: light drives photosynthesis, temperature controls enzyme rates, water and soil chemistry gate survival, and oxygen levels and pollution push sensitive species out entirely.
keyPoints: Low light slows plant growth, reducing food for herbivores and affecting the whole food chain.
Temperature controls enzyme-controlled reactions, so extremes reduce survival and reproduction.
Water availability and soil quality decide which plants, and therefore which animals, can persist.
Low oxygen in warm stagnant water kills fish, and pollution removes sensitive species such as lichens.

low.restatement: Light feeds plants, temperature tunes enzymes, water and soil select species, oxygen and pollution finish the rest.
low.analogy: A set of dials on a fish tank — each dial set wrong removes its own set of residents.
low.examPointer: Attach a consequence to each factor: light to food chains, temperature to enzymes, pH to soils, oxygen to water.

medium.restatement: Each factor bites through a mechanism: shade cuts photosynthesis so herbivores starve; heat and cold denature enzyme performance, limiting survival and reproduction; soil minerals and pH select the plant community; warm stagnant water holds little oxygen; and sulfur dioxide pollution wipes out lichens that indicate clean air.
medium.analogy: A hiring committee of six, each rejecting candidates for a different missing qualification.
medium.examPointer: Use the paired examples — polar bears and temperature, cacti and water, lichens and pollution — as ready-made evidence.

check.stem: Why does low light shrink a woodland food chain from the bottom?

options.text: Because photosynthesis slows, so plants yield less food for herbivores
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

options.text: Because herbivores dislike shade
options.explanation: The effect starts with plant growth, not herbivore taste.

options.text: Because light kills insects
options.explanation: Light does not kill insects at low intensity.

options.text: Because soil washes away
options.explanation: Soil loss is a separate factor.

check.stem: How does temperature act on survival?

options.text: It sets the rate of enzyme-controlled reactions, and extremes reduce survival
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: It changes the number of bones
options.explanation: Skeletal counts do not shift with temperature.

options.text: It only matters to reptiles
options.explanation: All organisms carry enzymes affected by temperature.

options.text: It affects plants but never animals
options.explanation: Animal enzymes are just as temperature-sensitive.

check.stem: Why can cacti store water in deserts while amphibians cannot?

options.text: Cacti store water and cut losses, while amphibians need moist conditions to reproduce
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: Cacti drink morning dew faster
options.explanation: Water storage and reduced loss are the stated adaptations.

options.text: Amphibians fear sunlight only
options.explanation: Moisture for reproduction is the deciding factor.

options.text: Deserts lack predators for cacti
options.explanation: Predation is not the mechanism here.

check.stem: What happens to fish in warm stagnant ponds?

options.text: Oxygen drops, so fish die or migrate to better-oxygenated water
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

options.text: Fish grow extra gills
options.explanation: No anatomical change is described.

options.text: Fish switch to breathing air
options.explanation: Fish cannot simply switch to air breathing.

options.text: The pond becomes saltier
options.explanation: Salinity is a different abiotic factor.

check.stem: Why do lichens indicate clean air?

options.text: Because sulfur dioxide pollution removes them, so their presence signals clean air
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: Because lichens feed on pollution
options.explanation: Pollution kills them; they do not feed on it.

options.text: Because lichens need city noise
options.explanation: Noise is irrelevant to lichens.

options.text: Because lichens grow only in cities
options.explanation: They thrive in clean air, the opposite.

check.stem: State one abiotic factor that affects plant growth in forests.
check.modelAnswer: Light intensity affects plant growth, since low light slows photosynthesis and reduces the food available to herbivores.

check.stem: Name the abiotic factor that limits polar bears to cold regions.
check.modelAnswer: Temperature limits polar bears to cold regions, where their thick fur and fat layer suit survival.

check.stem: Explain why soil pH shapes which plants grow on moorland.
check.modelAnswer: Soil pH shapes plant growth because acidic moorland suits heather while grasses and many crops fail, which then decides which animals the habitat can feed.

check.stem: A factory releases sulfur dioxide near a woodland. Predict the lichen population.
check.modelAnswer: The lichen population falls because lichens are sensitive to sulfur dioxide, so polluted air removes them while tolerant species persist.

lessons.title: Living Pressures
sourceHeadings: How biotic factors affect the population size and distribution of organisms
lessons.opening: Living neighbours press just as hard as any drought: food availability sets population ceilings, new predators and pathogens crash unprepared populations, and competition lets a better-adapted species push another towards local extinction.
keyPoints: Food availability decides survival and reproduction, so scarce food shrinks populations.
A new predator can disrupt the balance and drive prey populations down.
A new pathogen can devastate populations with no immunity or resistance.
In competition, the better-adapted species outcompetes the other, which may decline or become extinct locally.

low.restatement: Food feeds populations, predators and diseases cut them, and competition crowns the better adapted.
low.analogy: A market where buyers (food) set the ceiling, thieves (predators) drain stock, sickness (pathogens) closes stalls, and rival chains (competition) squeeze out the weakest shop.
low.examPointer: Carry the case studies: grey squirrels versus red squirrels, ash dieback, foxes in Australia.

medium.restatement: Each living pressure has a documented outcome: richer food raises populations; the arrival of a predator such as the red fox in Australia collapses native prey; a pathogen like ash dieback sweeps through unprotected hosts; and competition from grey squirrels combines resource theft with disease to push red squirrels towards local extinction.
medium.analogy: A new restaurant opening that steals customers, poaches the staff and brings a food scare to the whole street.
medium.examPointer: For outcompetition answers, name the resource competed for and any disease carried — that is what full marks need.

check.stem: What happens to a population when its food supply rises?

options.text: Survival and reproduction improve, so the population increases
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

options.text: The population falls as crowding spreads disease
options.explanation: More food supports more organisms, not fewer.

options.text: Only predators benefit
options.explanation: The fed species itself gains first.

options.text: Nothing changes without rain
options.explanation: Food supply itself shifts population size.

check.stem: Why did the grey squirrel population push red squirrels into decline after arriving in the UK?

options.text: They take food and nesting sites from red squirrels and carry a virus
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: They hunted red squirrels directly
options.explanation: Competition and disease, not direct hunting, drove the decline.

options.text: They ate all the acorns before ripening
options.explanation: Wider food use, including unripe acorns, gave the advantage.

options.text: They poisoned the water supply
options.explanation: Water poisoning is not the documented mechanism.

check.stem: What made ash dieback disease so damaging for populations in Europe?

options.text: Ash populations had no resistance to the newly arrived fungus
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: Ash trees were already dying of drought
options.explanation: Drought is not the cause named for dieback spread.

options.text: The fungus killed all other trees too
options.explanation: The named host is ash, not every species.

options.text: Foresters planted infected seeds on purpose
options.explanation: Deliberate planting is not part of the account.

check.stem: When does the losing competitor face local extinction?

options.text: When its numbers fall too low to breed successfully
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

options.text: As soon as any competitor appears
options.explanation: Decline takes hold as competition bites, not instantly.

options.text: Only if humans remove it
options.explanation: The losing species can fade without human help.

options.text: When food becomes unlimited
options.explanation: Unlimited food would ease, not cause, extinction.

check.stem: Red foxes were introduced to Australia for hunting. Which population declined as the new predator spread?

options.text: Native small mammals and birds declined as the new predator spread
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: Native species adopted foxes as prey
options.explanation: Foxes are the predators, not the prey.

options.text: Foxes died out from the heat
options.explanation: Foxes established and spread widely.

options.text: Nothing changed for decades
options.explanation: The introduction caused marked declines.

check.stem: State one biotic factor that changes population size.
check.modelAnswer: Competition is a biotic factor, and the better-adapted species outcompetes the other, changing population size.

check.stem: Name the biotic factor illustrated by a new fungus entering a woodland.
check.modelAnswer: A new pathogen is the biotic factor, since the fungus infects populations with no resistance.

check.stem: Explain why a new predator hits prey harder than an established one.
check.modelAnswer: A new predator hits harder because the prey population has no shared history of balance with it, so numbers fall before any equilibrium forms.

check.stem: Grey squirrels carry a virus red squirrels resist poorly. State two pressures on red squirrels.
check.modelAnswer: Red squirrels face competition for food and nesting sites plus disease from the virus, so both biotic pressures drive their decline.

glossary.definition: A non-living part of the environment, such as temperature or light intensity.
A living pressure within the environment, such as competition, predation or disease.
The struggle between organisms for the same resources, won by the better adapted.
A disease-causing organism that can devastate populations with no resistance.
To win the struggle for resources so thoroughly that another species declines.
